headline: Ministers expect lessons from Microsoft on the 365 outage as the cyber bill returns to the Commons
summary: A written answer on the 12–13 November Microsoft 365 outage puts Microsoft by name on the record, on the day MPs consider Lords amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill. The Lords opened an inquiry into UK compute (evidence by 15 January; first hearing today), a Lib Dem MP set out the case against two large Oxfordshire data centres, and peers warned of vendor lock-in on the NHS single patient record.

very_important.title: Government expects Microsoft to share lessons from the Microsoft 365 outage
very_important.who: Adam Dance (LD, Yeovil) to DCMS; answered by Ian Murray
very_important.body: Asked what assessment had been made of the cost to the UK economy of the 12–13 November Microsoft 365 outage, the minister said no assessment has been made because the impacts are still emerging. The Government expects Microsoft to share its lessons learned and will engage further on preventing such incidents and on faster remediation. He noted that cloud services are regulated under the NIS Regulations 2018 and that the Government expects a report to have been lodged with the regulator, the Information Commissioner.
very_important.why: Microsoft is named on the record as a resilience risk, with an explicit ministerial expectation of follow-up. It lands the day MPs debate Lords amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill, which updates the same NIS regime. Expect further questions; a proactive lessons-learned line to DCMS and DSIT would get ahead of them.

very_important.title: Cyber Security and Resilience Bill: Commons considers Lords amendments today
very_important.date: Tuesday 24 November, after the Armed Forces Bill
very_important.body: MPs will consider the Lords amendments to the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill, which brings more digital and managed service providers into the NIS regime and strengthens regulators' powers.
very_important.why: This is the statutory framework ministers cite for cloud outages (see above). Which Lords amendments the Government accepts or overturns sets the obligations Microsoft will operate under as a cloud and managed service provider.

very_important.title: Lords launch inquiry into the future of UK compute in the age of AI
very_important.date: Launched 23 Nov; evidence by 23:59, Friday 15 January 2027
very_important.body: The inquiry will examine the UK's compute and data-centre strategy and whether the UK can capture value in an AI economy dominated by US firms and overseas chip manufacturing. It will scrutinise the Compute Roadmap (at least 6 GW of AI-capable data-centre capacity by 2030), the AI Opportunities Action Plan, the AI Hardware Plan, the Sovereign AI Unit and the new Data Centre Covenant tests, and ask what 'sovereign AI' should mean. The call for evidence notes that Stargate UK and the US Technology Prosperity Deal have been paused or delayed. The first public session is today at 10:15.
very_important.why: This goes straight to Microsoft's core issues: hyperscale investment, grid and planning constraints, sovereignty and US dominance. A Microsoft submission, and possibly a witness slot, would put the company's numbers and position on the record before the committee frames the debate.

very_important.title: Lib Dem MP sets out the case against two large Oxfordshire data centres
very_important.who: Calum Miller (LD, Bicester and Woodstock); intervention by Jeremy Corbyn (Your Party, Islington North)
very_important.body: Miller said two proposed data centres in his constituency, 100 MW at Kidlington and 435 MW at Bicester, would together draw enough power for 1.4 million homes. He asked for details of the Chancellor's promised 'strict tests', a coherent national plan for data-centre siting, an independent assessment of projected AI electricity demand against grid capacity, and publication of impact assessments before priority grid access is granted. He described a consented warehouse quietly converted to a data centre under the same planning use class (B8) without local scrutiny. Corbyn asked whether this used the permitted-development 'loophole'.
very_important.why: This is the organised local-opposition argument (grid priority, bills, planning loopholes) put on the record in a money debate, with a cross-party echo. Expect it to recur in the Draft National Policy Statement for Data Centres consultation and in the Lords compute inquiry.

very_important.title: Peers warn of vendor lock-in on the NHS single patient record
very_important.who: Lord Kamall (Con), Lord Clement-Jones (LD); reply by Baroness Merron (DHSC)
very_important.date: Health Bill, Lords committee stage, 23 Nov
very_important.body: Lord Kamall cited the Commons Science, Innovation and Technology Committee's June warning of 'vendor lock-in' across government and the high cost of leaving long-term contracts, and asked where single patient record data would sit and whose laws would govern it, given that no supplier has been chosen and the link to the federated data platform is undecided. Lord Clement-Jones asked whether algorithms on the federated data platform would govern AI-generated patient summaries. The minister said future suppliers will not be permitted to use patient data for their own purposes, and promised to write.
very_important.why: This is a live national procurement framed by peers around sovereignty and lock-in. Positioning on data residency, portability and exit terms will matter well before a supplier is chosen.

debates.title: Peers press for statutory regulation of AI in healthcare; Government will consult in spring 2027
debates.who: Lord Tarassenko (CB), backed by Baroness Harding (Con), Lord Clement-Jones (LD) and Baroness Kidron (CB); reply by Baroness Hyde of Bemerton
debates.body: Amendment 172D would set a timetable for implementing the 44 accepted recommendations of the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare and require annual progress reports. Tarassenko noted that AI with a medical purpose is still regulated under 2002 medical-device rules. Kidron sought standards for mental-health chatbots, citing evidence that two in five children use a chatbot for advice or emotional support. The Government agreed that regulation must be proportionate and life-cycle based. It will consult in spring 2027 on classifying AI medical products and intends to lay draft regulations by the end of 2027.
debates.why: This sets the clock for the UK's first AI-specific product regulation in health. The chatbot strand overlaps with online safety and with consumer AI assistants.

debates.title: Single patient record: cyber security as critical national infrastructure
debates.who: Lord Markham (Con), Baroness Finlay (CB), Lord Kamall (Con)
debates.body: Lord Markham, a former health minister, warned of heightened cyber risk from concentrating patient data, recalling the attacks on London pathology providers. Baroness Finlay asked for the single patient record to be treated as critical national infrastructure, with the highest cyber security standards set in statute. Lord Kamall sought an assessment of interoperability, cyber security and operational resilience before regulations are made.
debates.why: Security and resilience requirements written into statute would shape any cloud architecture bid for the record.

debates.title: UK-EU Summit: Prime Minister promotes a new digital partnership
debates.who: The Prime Minister; question from Callum Anderson (Lab, Buckingham and Bletchley)
debates.body: The Prime Minister said the agreement proposes a digital partnership to deepen co-operation across digital and technology sectors, and that the UK is not joining the EU digital identity wallet. Callum Anderson asked how the partnership will consolidate the UK as a destination for technology investment and AI adoption; the Prime Minister called it a 'really big opportunity'.
debates.why: This is a new UK-EU channel on digital regulation and AI. Its terms of reference will matter for cross-border data and cloud services.

debates.title: Subscription contract rules approved, in force from 1 January
debates.who: Kate Dearden, Minister for the Future of Work; Second Delegated Legislation Committee
debates.body: The committee approved regulations implementing the subscriptions chapter of the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024: new information, reminder and easy-cancellation duties covering an estimated 155 million UK subscriptions. Subject to approval by Parliament, they commence on 1 January. The Conservatives did not oppose them. Graham Stuart (Con) asked for an early review and protection for small businesses and publishers.
debates.why: This applies to Xbox Game Pass, consumer Microsoft 365 and LinkedIn Premium. Compliance teams should confirm cancellation and renewal-reminder flows are ready for 1 January.

debates.title: Digital services tax raised in the Finance Bill debate
debates.body: Arguing for higher taxes on wealth and multinationals, Shockat Adam said the Government had not delivered the digital services tax it promised.
debates.why: A single mention, but it shows the digital services tax remains a live campaign line for MPs on the left.

questions.title: Data centres and planning: three directed into the national infrastructure regime, none yet decided
questions.who: Yasmin Qureshi (Lab), Wendy Morton (Con), Dr Ben Spencer (Con); answered by Matthew Pennycook (MHCLG)
questions.body: Four requests have been made to direct data-centre applications into the Nationally Significant Infrastructure Projects regime. One was withdrawn and three were granted; none has yet returned for decision. The department holds no data on applications with local authorities. Three of the five AI Growth Zones are in Scotland or Wales, where planning is devolved. The minister pointed to the Draft National Policy Statement for Data Centres, published by DBT on 28 October, whose consultation includes questions on the NSIP route, and said local authorities can still submit Local Impact Reports.
questions.why: This is the route large Microsoft sites could use, and the consultation is the place to shape it.

questions.title: Grid and water: Government backs Ofgem's crackdown on speculative data-centre connections
questions.who: Dame Chi Onwurah (Lab), answered by Michael Shanks (DESNZ); Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi (Lab, Slough), answered by Emma Hardy (Defra)
questions.body: On Ofgem's proposed Data Centre Commitment Fee, the minister said significant investments are being delayed by the volume of speculative data-centre projects in the grid queue, and that the Government strongly supports measures to make sure scarce capacity is held by credible, deliverable projects. The fee's design is for Ofgem. On Slough, Defra said new data centres will get water only where water companies judge resources sufficient, and are expected to minimise demand and use alternative sources.
questions.why: Connection fees and water conditions bear directly on Microsoft's UK build-out economics. Slough is a key cluster.

questions.title: 'Sovereign first' in place of Cloud First? DHSC defers to GDS
questions.who: Preet Kaur Gill (Lab, Birmingham Edgbaston), answered by James Frith (DHSC)
questions.body: She asked whether the Cloud First policy will be changed or replaced by a 'sovereign first' policy, and about sovereign versus public cloud for health innovation. DHSC said no assessment has been made and that the Government Digital Service leads on Cloud First.
questions.why: 'Sovereign first' framing is now appearing in Labour backbench questions. Watch GDS's next policy statement.

questions.title: AI in government: no central record of the models departments use
questions.who: Dr Ben Spencer (Con), answered by Stephanie Peacock and Kanishka Narayan; Viscount Camrose (Con)
questions.body: GDS holds no central record of the AI models departments use. It relies on the Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard, and further Cabinet Office activity is planned. The Prime Minister's AI Taskforce will not publish annual reports. Questions on Chinese AI models drew only general answers: discussions with US counterparts are not disclosed, and the AI Biosecurity Lab will assess security before approving any technology. Spencer has since tabled a question on whether the Cabinet Office uses Chinese open-weight models (UIN 45816).
questions.why: This is a sustained Conservative frontbench line on AI governance and supply-chain security in government, likely to lead to calls for model registers and procurement restrictions.

questions.title: Frontier AI whistleblowing: consultation closes 8 January
questions.who: Dame Chi Onwurah (Lab), answered by Kate Dearden (DBT)
questions.body: The Government has made no specific assessment of protections for workers at frontier AI companies who raise safety concerns. It is consulting, until 8 January, on whether the categories of protected disclosure remain appropriate for emerging technologies such as AI.
questions.why: This comes from the chair of the Commons Science, Innovation and Technology Committee. It is a hook for AI-safety-first campaigners, and the consultation is open.

questions.title: Online safety and AI: chatbots coming into scope; pressure on Ofcom over fraud
questions.who: Tanmanjeet Singh Dhesi (Lab), Dame Chi Onwurah (Lab); answered by Ian Murray (DCMS)
questions.body: Ministers noted that the Crime and Policing Act 2026 criminalised AI models optimised to create child sexual abuse material and took a power to bring currently unregulated AI chatbots within the Online Safety Act's illegal-content duties. On fraud, enforcement is for Ofcom, but the Government calls effective enforcement a priority.
questions.why: The chatbot power is the route by which consumer AI assistants could become regulated services.

questions.title: Competition: CMA investigating Meta's commercial terms
questions.who: Rebecca Long Bailey (Lab), answered by Kate Dearden (DBT)
questions.body: Asked whether the CMA should open a Strategic Market Status investigation into Meta's social media services, the minister said such decisions are for the CMA, which opened a Competition Act investigation into Meta's commercial terms on 30 October.
questions.why: Shows MPs pushing for wider use of the digital markets regime against Big Tech.

questions.title: Government cyber: Lord Clement-Jones presses on GOV.UK One Login
questions.who: Lord Clement-Jones (LD), five questions; Stuart Anderson (Con)
questions.body: Clement-Jones asked whether the officials assuring GOV.UK One Login's security have the right expertise, and why a GDS digital identity security role did not require cyber qualifications. That second question got the reply 'This is an operational matter'. On open-source software supply chains, the Cabinet Office said departments remain responsible, with the Government Commercial Agency enforcing baseline supplier security standards.
questions.why: Digital identity security is a continuing Lib Dem scrutiny theme, and supplier standards affect every government software contract.

questions.title: Also answered
questions.body: AI and music copyright: the Government supports licensing, as set out in its March report on AI and Copyright (HL5112). Liability of AI agents: existing law applies case by case (HL5114). EdTech and AI product safety certification: the consultation launched on 10 November covers data privacy and children's development (HL4692–HL4694).

questions.title: Newly tabled: series to watch
questions.body: Shivani Raja tabled six questions on AI in adult social care and children's data in public AI tools, covering evaluation metrics, cyber and data protection standards. James McMurdock tabled six on the powers of the proposed facial recognition watchdog. Also tabled: Dr Ben Spencer on Chinese open-weight models in the Cabinet Office; Lord Taylor of Warwick on AI companion apps and on AI X-ray software; Luke Akehurst (Lab) on the role of digital terrestrial TV during a major cyber incident; and Afzal Khan (Lab) on Online Safety Act business disruption orders for unpaid fines.
questions.why: The Raja series in particular asks what standards AI tools must meet before processing sensitive public-sector data, which matters for Copilot deployments in local government.

committees.title: Public Accounts Committee publishes DCMS letter on Government Cyber Resilience
committees.who: Letter from the Permanent Secretary, DCMS, 18 November
committees.body: The letter responds to the committee's 24th report of session 2024–26, Government Cyber Resilience. Its contents were not reviewed for this edition because the PDF could not be read.
committees.why: Likely relevant to public-sector cloud and legacy IT risk. Worth reading in full.

committees.title: Public Accounts Committee: NS&I transformation programme correspondence
committees.who: NS&I interim chief executive; HM Treasury Permanent Secretary
committees.body: Letters on the Accounting Officer Assessment of NS&I's Business Transformation (formerly 'Rainbow') programme and on lessons learned.
committees.why: A reference case for government IT transformation risk and supplier dependency.

committees.title: Other committee notes
committees.body: Commons DCMS Committee membership: Alison Bennett replaces Cameron Thomas. Lords European Affairs Committee published a letter from Hamish Falconer (20 November) on the UK-EU Summit and the European Partnership Bill.

other.title: Treasury flags North Korea-linked remote IT workers in its proliferation financing risk assessment
other.who: Lucy Rigby, Economic Secretary to the Treasury
other.date: Written statement, 23 Nov (HCWS494; HLWS504 in the Lords)
other.body: The new National Risk Assessment of Proliferation Financing names emerging threats including cryptoassets, cyber-enabled activity and DPRK-linked remote IT workers who generate revenue and evade sanctions. It identifies North Korea and Iran as the most significant state actors.
other.why: Remote IT worker schemes run through recruitment platforms and cloud services. This is relevant to LinkedIn's and Microsoft's trust-and-safety work, and an opening to point to action already taken.

other.title: POST: How could quantum computers undermine digital security?
other.who: Parliamentary Office of Science and Technology
other.date: Latest on POST's home page (publication date not confirmed)
other.body: A briefing on the threat that quantum computing poses to current public-key encryption and on moves to post-quantum cryptography.
other.why: Relevant to cyber and encryption policy, and to Microsoft's quantum-safe and quantum programmes.

other.title: Libraries
other.body: No Commons or Lords Library publications on these topics in the period. The Lords Library's Health Bill briefing (7 October) is useful background to the single patient record debate.

coverage: Both Houses sat on Monday 23 November. Hansard read in full: Commons Chamber, Westminster Hall and General Committees; Lords Chamber (no Grand Committee record that day). Debates were screened by keyword and then read for relevance.

Committees: committee publications for 23 November across all committees, the Lords Science and Technology inquiry pages, and today's committee schedule. Hugh's named committees were not each checked individually on their own news pages.
Parliament Today: What's On for the Commons, Lords and committees on 24 November. The Order Paper and Lords Business were not read separately.

Not read: the Public Accounts Committee cyber resilience letter (PDF). The pre-fetched OneDrive file was not used; written questions came directly from the Parliament API via this repository's pipeline.
